paras: The threat against a Black federal marshal at Kingstree took place on election day, November 2, 1880, in Kingstree, Williamsburg County, South Carolina, when the state constable, Captain J. A. Kelley, announced that a colored U.S. marshal would be jailed if he tried to make any arrest. The marshal put away his badge and withdrew, and the day ended without reported violence, though a collision between white and Black residents was said to have been imminent. The account became known outside the state when a Washington Republican paper reprinted the local Kingstree Star's version under the heading "Red Shirt Tactics."

Kingstree was a polling place in South Carolina's First Congressional District, where the Republican Samuel Lee ran against the Democrat John S. Richardson. According to the Star, Lee had promised a "countless number" of federal marshals for the election, and the paper said the sheriff's supporters had been "incendiarized by Sam Lee & Co. last Friday." A Kingstree dispatch also claimed that Black voters at some other precincts stayed away from the polls because of a "lesson taught them early in the campaign," without describing that lesson.

By the Star's account, the voting went smoothly until visitors arrived from Scranton on the 11 o'clock freight train, causing a brief stir. When a Black man appeared as a U.S. marshal, the only one of those Lee had promised, Kelley announced that if he "attempted to make an arrest under any circumstances he was to be ignominiously jailed." The Star wrote that the resulting excitement ended with "the disappearance of the badge from the sight of all men" and what it called the marshal's "voluntary return" to private life.

Earlier that morning Sheriff Jacobs, who was serving as election supervisor, had said he could not also act as peace officer, which left the peace of the town to Kelley and his assistants. In the afternoon, according to the Star, Black men "came very near precipitating a row" when Democrats arrived from Graham's on the 4 o'clock passenger train. The election dispatch from Kingstree likewise reported that a collision between whites and blacks was at one time imminent but that the day passed without violence, with more than 900 votes cast and a Republican majority at the box.

No report of any arrest, charge or inquiry over Kelley's threat appears in the coverage. In December, Lee served notice that he would contest Richardson's seat, charging among other things that deputy marshals throughout the district had been "obstructed, hindered, and prevented" by Richardson's supporters and that ballots had been manipulated at Kingstree.

South Carolina papers printed the Kingstree election dispatch on November 4 in the Winnsboro News and Herald and, in shorter form, the Anderson Intelligencer, mentioning only the near-collision and praising the "possum" policy of Black non-voting. The Yorkville Enquirer turned the charge around, claiming on November 11 that Kingstree's Black voters had hidden their arms on the outskirts of town, "as the volleys after dark proved."

The threat to the marshal reached readers only through the Kingstree Star, whose own approving account the National Republican of Washington reprinted on November 8 as a "pleasant account of red shirt management," letting the Democratic paper's words serve as evidence of intimidation. No account from the marshal himself or from Black voters at Kingstree appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Threat against a Black federal marshal at Kingstree, 1880
bases: The Kingstree Star, reprinted in A3, says the state constable announced that a colored U.S. marshal would be jailed if he made any arrest, after which the marshal put away his badge; no one was reported hurt (A1, A3).

The threat to the marshal appears only in the Star account reprinted by A3; the Kingstree dispatch (A1, A2) independently reports a near-collision between whites and Blacks that day but does not mention the marshal.

accounts.label: Kingstree Star (local Democratic paper), via the National Republican
accounts.gist: Kelley announced that the colored marshal would be jailed if he attempted an arrest; the badge vanished and the marshal 'voluntarily' returned to private life. The Star blamed Black men, 'incendiarized' by Sam Lee, for nearly starting a row in the afternoon and credited white citizens with keeping order.

accounts.label: Kingstree election dispatch
accounts.gist: The election passed without violence, though a collision between whites and blacks was at one time imminent; over 900 votes were polled with a Republican majority at the box.

accounts.label: Yorkville Enquirer election items
accounts.gist: Black voters at Kingstree came to the polls with their arms hidden on the outskirts of town, 'as the volleys after dark proved.'

accounts.label: Samuel Lee's contest notice
accounts.gist: Deputy marshals throughout the district were obstructed and hindered by Richardson's partisans; ballots at Kingstree were manipulated.

framing.detail: The Republican National Republican used the Star's own boastful account as evidence against Democrats, heading it 'Red Shirt Tactics' and calling it a 'pleasant account of red shirt management', while the reprinted Star text itself approved of the threat.
South Carolina Democratic dispatches reported a quiet election at Kingstree with an imminent racial collision and praised Black non-voting as the 'possum' policy learned from an earlier 'lesson'.
The Yorkville Enquirer cast Kingstree's Black voters as the armed threat, citing volleys after dark.

versions.value: Black voters, stirred up by Sam Lee, nearly started a row and hid arms outside town
A state constable threatened to jail the only federal marshal, who withdrew (the Star's own account, presented by the National Republican as red-shirt intimidation)

conflicts.note: All accounts come from white papers; no account from the marshal or Black voters was found.

record_check.record: about twenty armed private men were raised, then returned
record_check.dossier: No source mentions twenty armed men; the man who 'returned to private life' was the marshal himself, after the threat.
Threat only; no armed gathering by Kelley is reported (the Yorkville Enquirer alleges Black voters hid arms).
Captain J. A. Kelley, state constable, and his assistants.
Three reports of the day at Kingstree (A1, A2, A3) plus a passing Yorkville item.
